content: 1. Criminalizing abortion constitutes a violation of international human rights law (IHRL). Such laws are incompatible with the right to be free from torture, cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment, as outlined in the 2016 report by the Special Rapporteur on Torture to the Human Rights Council (UN Doc. A/HRC/31/57). 2. Laws regulating abortion must be evidence-based and proportionate. This principle is emphasized in the 2011 interim report by the Special Rapporteur on the right to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health to the General Assembly (UN Doc. A/66/254). 3. Criminal laws that penalize or restrict abortion are impermissible restrictions on women’s rights to health. They perpetuate unsafe conditions and violate the right to health and safety, as noted in the 2011 interim report by the Special Rapporteur on the right to health (UN Doc. A/66/254). 4. The criminal prohibition of pregnancy termination violates women’s rights to health and safety. This is highlighted in the 2016 report of the United Nations Working Group on discrimination against women in law and practice (UN Doc. A/HRC/32/44). 5. States must remove barriers to the provision of safe abortion care and ensure that healthcare providers can perform their duties without undue interference, intimidation, or restrictions. This is emphasized in the 2018 report by the Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary, or arbitrary executions to the General Assembly (UN Doc. A/73/314). 6. At a minimum, abortion must be available, accessible, and of good quality in cases where the life or health of the woman is at risk, when the pregnancy results from rape or incest, or in cases of severe and fatal fetal impairment. This is outlined in the 2011 interim report by the Special Rapporteur on the right to health (UN Doc. A/66/254) and the 2018 report by the Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions (UN Doc. A/73/314). 7. Abortion should be decriminalized, and access to safe and legal abortion must be assured, at least in cases of rape, incest, severe or fatal fetal impairment, or when the life or physical or mental health of the woman is at risk. This is emphasized in the 2016 report by the Special Rapporteur on Torture to the Human Rights Council (UN Doc. A/HRC/31/57). 8. States must provide safe, legal, and effective access to abortion when the life and health of the pregnant woman are at risk. This is supported by the Human Rights Committee’s General Comment No. 36 on Article 6 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (2018, UN Doc. CCPR/C/GC/36). 9. States must ensure access to abortion in cases where carrying a pregnancy to term would cause substantial pain or suffering, particularly in cases of rape or non-viable pregnancies. This is also emphasized in the Human Rights Committee’s General Comment No. 36 (2018, UN Doc. CCPR/C/GC/36). 10. Denial of abortion, healthcare, and bereavement support in cases of fatal fetal diagnoses causes suffering of sufficient intensity to violate the right to be free from torture, cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment. This is highlighted in the Human Rights Committee’s decisions in Whelan v. Ireland (2017, UN Doc. CCPR/C/11/D/2425/2014) and Mellett v. Ireland (2016, UN Doc. CCPR/C/116/D/2324/2013). 11. States must ensure that abortion and abortion-related healthcare are available in cases of fatal fetal anomalies. This is supported by the Human Rights Committee’s decisions in Whelan v. Ireland and Mellett v. Ireland. 12. The obligation to respect the right to sexual and reproductive health requires states to refrain from interfering with individuals’ exercise of this right. This includes reforming laws that impede access to sexual and reproductive health, such as laws criminalizing abortion. This is emphasized in the 2021 report by the Special Rapporteur on the right to health during the COVID-19 pandemic (UN Doc. A/76/172). 13. States must ensure adequate access to essential medicines in an affordable and non-discriminatory manner. This is outlined in the Committee on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights (CESCR) General Comment No. 14 on the right to health (2000, UN Doc. 12/2000/4). 14. Access to essential medicines, including for vulnerable and marginalized groups, must not be impeded by political, legal, or cultural considerations. This is emphasized in the 2013 interim report by the Special Rapporteur on the right to health (UN Doc. A/HRC/23/42). 15. States must ensure equality and non-discrimination in the provision of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, including abortion. This is supported by the Human Rights Committee’s General Comment No. 36 (2018, UN Doc. CCPR/C/GC/36) and the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) General Comment No. 15 (2013, UN Doc. CRC/C/GC/15). 16. Health systems and services must meet the specific sexual and reproductive health needs of adolescents, including safe abortion. This is emphasized in the CRC General Comment No. 15 (2013, UN Doc. CRC/C/GC/15). 17. Adolescents must have access to non-discriminatory, confidential, and responsive sexual and reproductive health services, including safe abortion. This is highlighted in the 2016 report by the Special Rapporteur on the right to health (UN Doc. A/HRC/32/32). 18. Health services for adolescents should include HIV-related information, testing, diagnostics, care, and treatment, as well as information on contraception, condom use, safe abortion, and post-abortion care. This is emphasized in the 2021 report by the Special Rapporteur on the right to health during the COVID-19 pandemic (UN Doc. A/76/172). 19. Criminalizing abortion results in discrimination against women. This is highlighted in the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) General Recommendation No. 33 on women’s access to justice (2015, UN Doc. CEDAW/C/GC/33). 20. Criminalizing behaviors that can only be undertaken by women, such as abortion, is inherently discriminatory. Termination of pregnancy should be decriminalized. This is emphasized in the 2016 report of the United Nations Working Group on discrimination against women in law and practice (UN Doc. A/HRC/32/44). 21. Criminalizing abortion disproportionately affects economically disadvantaged women, constituting severe discrimination. This is highlighted in the 2016 report of the United Nations Working Group on discrimination against women in law and practice (UN Doc. A/HRC/32/44). 22. States should allow pregnant girls and adolescents to terminate pregnancies to enable them to complete their education. This is emphasized in the 2016 report of the United Nations Working Group on discrimination against women in law and practice (UN Doc. A/HRC/32/44). 23. Criminalizing abortion is a form of gender-based violence that may amount to cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment. States must repeal all discriminatory provisions, including those criminalizing abortion. This is emphasized in CEDAW General Recommendation No. 35 on gender-based violence against women (2017, UN Doc. CEDAW/C/GC/35).
